pairs.question: Quis poenae modus aut pereundi terminus, oro, Aeneadis erit, et quando terrasque fretumque emensis sedisse dabis? cur pellere nostros a te concessa Poenus parat urbe nepotes? Alpibus imposuit Libyam finemque minatur imperio. casus metuit iam Roma Sagunti. quo Troiae extremos cineres sacramque ruinam Assaracique larem et Vestae secreta feramus? da sedem, genitor, tutisque iacere. parumne est exilia errantis totum quaesisse per orbem? anne iterum capta repetentur Pergama Roma?
pairs.answer: Pelle metus, neu te Tyriae conamina gentis turbarint, Cytherea: tenet longumque tenebit Tarpeias arces sanguis tuus.
pairs.derivation: Venus's entire speech (3.559-569) is one extended fearful plea built around genuine interrogatives ('Quis poenae modus... erit?', 'cur pellere... parat...?', 'quo... feramus?', 'parumne est...?', 'anne iterum... repetentur Pergama Roma?'); quoted whole and contiguous as the question. The framing narration 'At Venus, ancipiti mentem labefacta timore, adfatur genitorem et rumpit maesta querelas' (3.557-558) before it and 'His Venus, et contra genitor sic deinde profatur' (3.570) after it are dropped as speech tags; 'oro' is kept because it is embedded inside the question, not a detachable tag. Jupiter's reply opens by directly answering her fear: the answer window is his first sentence, 'Pelle metus... sanguis tuus.' (3.571-573, to the first full stop), and stops before 'hac ego Martis mole uiros spectare paro...' where he turns from reassurance to the long prophecy of Rome's destiny. Every-five-line verse numbers, the title lines, and the trailing Latin-Library footer were stripped.
